chapterTitle: A Priest Called by God, a People Called to Grow Up
themeTitle: “He Learned Obedience by the Things Which He Suffered”

scripture.text: For every high priest, being taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.
scripture.understanding: Now the writer explains what a high priest is. πᾶς γὰρ ἀρχιερεὺς ἐξ ἀνθρώπων λαμβανόμενος, “For every high priest, being taken from among men” — he must be human, one of the people. ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καθίσταται τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν, “is appointed for men in things pertaining to God” — he stands between them and God. ἵνα προσφέρῃ δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν, “that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.” Three members of the new offering family: προσφέρω, to bring near and offer; δῶρον, a gift; θυσία, a slain sacrifice.

scripture.text: The high priest can deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, because he himself is also surrounded with weakness.
scripture.understanding: μετριοπαθεῖν δυνάμενος, “The high priest can deal gently” — μετριοπαθέω, to keep one's feelings in proportion: neither harsh anger nor soft indulgence. τοῖς ἀγνοοῦσιν καὶ πλανωμένοις, “with those who are ignorant and going astray” — sins of weakness and wandering, not defiant rebellion. ἐπεὶ καὶ αὐτὸς περίκειται ἀσθένειαν, “because he himself is also surrounded with weakness” — weakness wrapped around him like a garment.

scripture.text: Because of this, he must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself.
scripture.understanding: καὶ δι᾽ αὐτὴν ὀφείλει, “Because of this, he must” — the human high priest had a problem: he was a sinner too. καθὼς περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ, οὕτως καὶ περὶ αὑτοῦ προσφέρειν περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν, “offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself.” On the Day of Atonement, Aaron first offered a bull for his own sin, then a goat for the people (Leviticus 16). Jesus did not need to (7:27).

scripture.text: Nobody takes this honor on himself, but he is called by God, just like Aaron was.
scripture.understanding: καὶ οὐχ ἑαυτῷ τις λαμβάνει τὴν τιμήν, “Nobody takes this honor on himself,” ἀλλὰ καλούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, καθώσπερ καὶ Ἀαρών, “but he is called by God, just like Aaron was.” Those who grabbed priestly power for themselves — Korah's rebels, King Uzziah burning incense — were judged. The priesthood is a calling, not a career.

scripture.text: So also Christ didn’t glorify himself to be made a high priest, but it was he who said to him, “You are my Son. Today I have become your father.”
scripture.understanding: οὕτως καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς οὐχ ἑαυτὸν ἐδόξασεν γενηθῆναι ἀρχιερέα, “So also Christ didn’t glorify himself to be made a high priest.” ἀλλ᾽ ὁ λαλήσας πρὸς αὐτόν, “but it was he who said to him” — the Father appointed Him — and the writer quotes Psalm 2 again, as in 1:5: “You are my Son. Today I have become your father.” σήμερον from the time family. The One appointed priest is first of all the Son.

scripture.text: As he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
scripture.understanding: καθὼς καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγει, “As he says also in another place” — Psalm 110, the same psalm as 1:13. “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.” εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα from the time family: unending. Melchizedek was the mysterious king-priest of Salem who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14). Jesus is a priest not by descent from Aaron but by God's oath, in a different and greater order. Chapter 7 will explain.

scripture.text: He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear,
scripture.understanding: ὃς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ, “He, in the days of his flesh” — His earthly life of weakness. δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας, “having offered up prayers and petitions” — two pray-family words: δέησις, a request born of need, and ἱκετηρία, the plea of a suppliant (originally the olive branch held out by someone begging for mercy). μετὰ κραυγῆς ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ δακρύων, “with strong crying and tears” — Gethsemane. πρὸς τὸν δυνάμενον σῴζειν αὐτὸν ἐκ θανάτου, “to him who was able to save him from death.” καὶ εἰσακουσθεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας, “and having been heard for his godly fear” — εὐλάβεια, added to the godliness family: reverent awe. He was heard: not spared from dying, but saved out of death by resurrection.

scripture.text: though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.
scripture.understanding: καίπερ ὢν υἱός, “though he was a Son” — though He was God's eternal Son. ἔμαθεν ἀφ᾽ ὧν ἔπαθεν τὴν ὑπακοήν, “yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” A Greek wordplay: ἔμαθεν, ‘he learned’; ἔπαθεν, ‘he suffered’. He was never disobedient; but as a man He learned by experience what obedience costs, step by step, all the way to the cross.

scripture.text: Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation,
scripture.understanding: καὶ τελειωθείς, “Having been made perfect” — τελειόω from the perfect family: brought to the goal, fully qualified as Saviour through His suffering and obedience (as in 2:10). ἐγένετο πᾶσιν τοῖς ὑπακούουσιν αὐτῷ αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίου, “he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation.” ‘Author’ here is αἴτιος, the source or cause — a different word from ἀρχηγός, the pioneer, in 2:10 (both are in the new author family). He who obeyed (v. 8) saves those who obey Him.

scripture.text: named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
scripture.understanding: προσαγορευθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀρχιερεὺς κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισέδεκ, “named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.” προσαγορεύω, to address formally, to hail by a title. The Father Himself publicly gave Him the title.

scripture.text: About him we have many words to say, and hard to interpret, seeing you have become dull of hearing.
scripture.understanding: The writer pauses before explaining Melchizedek. περὶ οὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος καὶ δυσερμήνευτος λέγειν, “About him we have many words to say, and hard to interpret” — λόγος from the word family. The difficulty is not in the subject but in the hearers: ἐπεὶ νωθροὶ γεγόνατε ταῖς ἀκοαῖς, “seeing you have become dull of hearing.” νωθρός means sluggish, lazy; ‘have become’ shows they were not always like this. This begins the third warning passage.

scripture.text: For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food.
scripture.understanding: καὶ γὰρ ὀφείλοντες εἶναι διδάσκαλοι διὰ τὸν χρόνον, “For although by this time you should be teachers” — χρόνος from the time family: given how long they had believed. πάλιν χρείαν ἔχετε τοῦ διδάσκειν ὑμᾶς τινὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ θεοῦ, “you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God” — στοιχεῖα, the ABCs; λόγια, God's oracles. γάλακτος, ‘milk’, καὶ οὐ στερεᾶς τροφῆς, ‘and not solid food’.

scripture.text: For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby.
scripture.understanding: πᾶς γὰρ ὁ μετέχων γάλακτος ἄπειρος λόγου δικαιοσύνης, “For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness” — ἄπειρος, without experience, untested. The ‘word of righteousness’ may mean teaching about righteousness, or the skill to live rightly. νήπιος γάρ ἐστιν, “for he is a baby.” There is nothing wrong with being a baby — at first. The tragedy is remaining one.

scripture.text: But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.
scripture.understanding: τελείων δέ ἐστιν ἡ στερεὰ τροφή, “But solid food is for those who are full grown” — τέλειος from the perfect family: mature, having reached the goal. Note the pattern: Christ was ‘made perfect’ (τελειόω, v. 9); believers are to be ‘full grown’ (τέλειος); and the next verse calls them on to ‘perfection’ (τελειότης, 6:1). τῶν διὰ τὴν ἕξιν τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα ἐχόντων, “who by reason of use have their senses exercised” — γυμνάζω, trained like an athlete (our ‘gymnasium’), by habit. πρὸς διάκρισιν καλοῦ τε καὶ κακοῦ, “to discern good and evil” — καλός from the good family and κακός from the evil family. Maturity is the trained ability to tell them apart.

visualMeditations.title: The Garden at Night
visualMeditations.image: Picture an olive grove on a hillside outside Jerusalem at night. The city sleeps below. A few men lie asleep under the trees. A short distance away, one Man kneels, then falls on His face on the ground. His shoulders shake; His voice rises in loud cries; His tears fall on the dirt. He is pleading with His Father. And then, through the tears, comes the quiet surrender: ‘Not what I desire, but what you desire.’
visualMeditations.meaning: “He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear” (v. 7), “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (v. 8). Your High Priest knows what it is to pray in agony and to obey at great cost. He was heard — not by escaping death, but by being raised from it. Bring your tears to Him.

visualMeditations.title: Milk and Solid Food
visualMeditations.image: Picture a nursery with a baby in a high chair, happily drinking milk. That is beautiful. Then picture the same room years later: a grown man, tall and strong, sitting in the same high chair, still drinking from a bottle, unable to chew a meal, never having learned to feed himself. What was lovely at the beginning has become a tragedy.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food” (v. 12). Spiritual infancy is normal at first, but it is not meant to last. Growth comes by practice: “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (v. 14). Ask the Spirit where you need to move from milk to solid food.

visualMeditations.title: The Trained Palate
visualMeditations.image: Picture an expert wine taster or a master chef. A beginner can only tell whether something is sweet or sour. The expert can identify each ingredient, notice the faintest note of spoilage, and tell at once whether a dish is safe and good. That skill did not come in a day; it came from thousands of tastings, careful attention and practice.
visualMeditations.meaning: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (v. 14). Spiritual discernment is a trained skill. It grows as you feed on God's word and practise obeying it, until you can sense quickly what is good and what is harmful. Ask the Spirit to train your senses through daily use.

structure.label: What a High Priest Must Be (v. 1-4)
structure.body: Every high priest is taken from among people to represent them before God and offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; he can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward because he too is weak, must offer for his own sins as well as the people's, and does not take the honour for himself but is called by God, as Aaron was.

structure.label: Christ, the Called and Perfected Priest (v. 5-10)
structure.body: Christ did not glorify Himself but was appointed by the One who called Him Son and declared Him a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek; in His earthly life He offered prayers and pleas with loud cries and tears to the One able to save Him from death, was heard because of His reverence, learned obedience through suffering, and, having been perfected, became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey Him.

structure.label: The Third Warning: Grow Up (v. 11-14)
structure.body: There is much to say about Melchizedek, but it is hard to explain because the readers have become sluggish in hearing; though they ought to be teachers by now, they need milk again instead of solid food, which belongs to the mature whose senses are trained by practice to distinguish good from evil.

sections.heading: What Makes a High Priest
paragraphs: Chapter 5 lays out the qualifications of a high priest. He must be human: “For every high priest, being taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins” (v. 1). He must be compassionate: he “can deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, because he himself is also surrounded with weakness” (v. 2). And he must be appointed: “Nobody takes this honor on himself, but he is called by God, just like Aaron was” (v. 4).

Jesus meets every qualification. He is truly human, having shared our flesh and blood (2:14). He can deal gently with the weak, because He knows weakness from the inside (4:15). And He was appointed by God: “So also Christ didn’t glorify himself to be made a high priest” (v. 5). The Father who called Him Son also declared, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek” (v. 6).

But Jesus surpasses the Aaronic priests at one crucial point. They had to offer sacrifices “for the people, as well as for himself” (v. 3), because they were sinners. Jesus never needed to. He was “tempted like we are, yet without sin” (4:15). He is a High Priest who fully understands our weakness and yet has none of our guilt.

sections.heading: Loud Cries and Tears
paragraphs: Verses 7–8 give one of the most moving pictures of Jesus in Scripture: “He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear” (v. 7). This is Gethsemane, where Jesus prayed, “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Mark 14:36). Luke adds that “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43).

Was He heard? He still went to the cross. But He was heard in the deepest way: God did not spare Him from death but saved Him out of death by raising Him. Peter preached that God “raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it” (Acts 2:24). And the reason He was heard was His εὐλάβεια, His reverent submission — a word this study adds to the godliness family.

“though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (v. 8). Jesus was never disobedient. But as a man He learned by experience the cost of obedience, all the way to death. Paul says He became “obedient to death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8). “Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation” (v. 9). His perfect obedience made Him the source of salvation for all who trust and obey Him.

sections.heading: From Milk to Solid Food
paragraphs: The writer wants to explain the deep truth of Christ's Melchizedek priesthood, but he stops short: “About him we have many words to say, and hard to interpret, seeing you have become dull of hearing” (v. 11). The problem is not the subject but the listeners. They have ‘become’ dull: they were not always this way. This is the third warning passage of the letter. Drift (2:1), hardness (3:12) and now dullness are steps on the same downward path.

Their spiritual growth has stalled: “For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food” (v. 12). Paul had to tell the Corinthians the same: “I fed you with milk, not with meat; for you weren’t yet ready” (1 Corinthians 3:2). Milk is good for babies; Peter tells new believers to “long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow” (1 Peter 2:2). But the goal is to grow.

Maturity is defined practically: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (v. 14). The perfect-family word τέλειος describes believers who have reached the goal of growth. The way there is practice — γυμνάζω, training like an athlete. Paul's goal for the church was “to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13), so “that we may no longer be children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14).

ntConnection.heading: The Obedient Son and the Growing Church
paragraphs: Jesus' obedience is central to the gospel. He said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34), and “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). Paul contrasts Adam and Christ: “For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). Facing the cross, Jesus said, “Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time?’ But for this cause I came to this time” (John 12:27).

His appointment as priest by God's word is repeated in Hebrews: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 7:17), and the oath “appoints a Son forever who has been perfected” (Hebrews 7:28). He is the “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). And His suffering leaves an example: “Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21).

The call to grow appears throughout the New Testament. “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 3:18). Paul longed for believers to “attain to the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man” (Ephesians 4:13). Growth is not optional; it is the normal life of those who feed on God's word and practise it.

lexicon.english: Deal gently / be moderate in feeling
lexicon.insight: Strong's: “to be moderate in passion, i.e. gentle (to treat indulgently).” It appears only here in the New Testament. Greek philosophers used it for the middle path between cold indifference and uncontrolled emotion. A good priest neither explodes in anger at the wayward nor excuses their sin; he bears with them patiently, because he knows his own weakness. Jesus does this perfectly.

Strong's: “intreaty.” It comes from ἱκέτης, a suppliant, and originally referred to the olive branch wrapped in wool that a suppliant held out when begging for mercy. It appears only here in the New Testament, describing Jesus' prayers in Gethsemane. This study adds it to the pray family beside δέησις (a request born of need). Jesus prayed as a suppliant, in agony, yet in perfect trust.

Strong's: “properly, caution, i.e. (religiously) reverence (piety); by implication, dread (concretely).” It describes careful, reverent awe toward God. Jesus was heard because of it (5:7), and believers are to serve God ‘with reverence and awe’ (12:28). English ‘godly’ hides both εὐσεβής-words and this one, so this study adds it to the godliness family.

Strong's: “causative, i.e. (concretely) a causer.” It means the one from whom something comes. In Hebrews 5:9 the WEB renders it ‘author’, but it is a different word from ἀρχηγός, also rendered ‘author’ in 2:10 and 12:2. ἀρχηγός is the pioneer who goes first; αἴτιος is the source of salvation. This study tags both in the new author family.

Strong's: “to practise naked (in the games), i.e. train (figuratively).” Greek athletes trained unclothed in the γυμνάσιον, the root of our ‘gymnasium’. Paul tells Timothy to ‘exercise yourself toward godliness’ with this word. Spiritual discernment is not instant; it is built through repeated practice, like an athlete's strength. Hebrews uses it again of discipline that trains us (12:11).

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit shows you a High Priest who prayed with tears, and calls you to grow up in Him.

items.title: He Prayed With Tears
items.body: Your High Priest knows what it is to plead with God in anguish. The Spirit invites you to bring Him your loud cries and tears without shame. He was heard because of His reverent submission; ask the Spirit to give you the same trust that says, ‘Not my will, but yours.’

items.title: Obedience Is Learned
items.body: Jesus learned obedience through suffering. The Spirit may be teaching you obedience through hardship too. Rather than resent it, ask Him what He is teaching you, and how this season can deepen your trust and your willingness to follow.

items.title: Time to Grow
items.body: The Spirit is calling you beyond spiritual infancy. Where have you settled for milk — the basics, others' teaching, emotional experiences — when you could be feeding on solid food and training your discernment? Ask Him to stir an appetite for deeper truth and to give you opportunities to practise it.

audit.title: The Gentleness Check
audit.body: How do you respond to people who are ignorant or straying? Do you lean toward harshness or toward excusing sin? Ask God for the balanced gentleness of verse 2.

audit.title: The Prayer Check
audit.body: When did you last pray with real earnestness about something? Bring one deep burden to God this week with honesty and reverence (v. 7).

audit.title: The Growth Check
audit.body: Compared with a few years ago, are you growing in understanding and discernment, or still needing the basics (vv. 12–14)? Write down one step toward solid food.

practices.title: A Solid-Food Reading Plan
practices.body: Choose one meaty book of the Bible (perhaps Hebrews itself) and study it slowly over the next two months with a good study aid. Read a chapter each week several times, write a summary, list questions, and discuss them with a friend. Aim to be able to explain its main teaching to someone else — moving toward being a teacher (v. 12).

practices.title: Discernment Training
practices.body: Each day for a month, choose one decision, message or piece of media you encounter and ask: ‘What is good here, and what is harmful?’ Test it against Scripture. Write a short note. Over time your senses will be trained by practice to discern good and evil (v. 14).

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, You are my great High Priest, taken from among humanity and appointed by the Father. Thank You that You deal gently with me when I am ignorant and wandering, because You understand weakness. You did not glorify Yourself; the Father called You His Son and named You a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. In the days of Your flesh You prayed with loud cries and tears, and You were heard because of Your reverent submission. Though You were the Son, You learned obedience through what You suffered. Thank You that You were made perfect and became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey You. Help me to obey You. Forgive me for becoming dull of hearing. Stir in me a hunger for solid food. Train my senses by practice to discern good and evil. Help me grow until I can teach others what You have taught me. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”

storyConnections.title: Aaron Called to Be High Priest
storyConnections.summary: God told Moses to bring his brother Aaron and Aaron's sons near from among the Israelites to serve as priests. Later, Korah and a group of leaders challenged Aaron's right to the priesthood, claiming that the whole community was holy. God judged the rebels, and then confirmed Aaron's calling by causing his staff, among the staffs of all the tribes, to sprout, blossom and produce almonds overnight. Hebrews 5:4 recalls this: ‘Nobody takes this honor on himself, but he is called by God, just like Aaron was.’ Jesus, too, did not take the priesthood for Himself; the Father appointed Him.

storyConnections.title: Jesus in Gethsemane
storyConnections.summary: After the Last Supper, Jesus went with His disciples to the Mount of Olives. Taking Peter, James and John further, He began to be deeply distressed. He prayed, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). An angel came to strengthen Him, and in His agony He prayed even more earnestly. Three times He returned to find the disciples sleeping. Then He rose to face His betrayer. Hebrews 5:7 describes this night: prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death.

storyConnections.title: Melchizedek Blesses Abraham
storyConnections.summary: After Abraham rescued his nephew Lot by defeating four kings, he was met by Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High. Melchizedek brought out bread and wine and blessed Abraham by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth. Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. Centuries later, Psalm 110 promised a king who would be ‘a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek’. Hebrews 5–7 shows that Jesus is that priest: not from Aaron's line, but greater, a king-priest appointed by God's oath.
